items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I had been receiving letters and telegrams from Rodger Kay asking me to hurry back to New York because he was going to take a combo into a new club and wanted me to join him.

ctx.x: A few more dates in Tennessee and North Carolina and then a week in Detroit at the Paradise theatre where I gave my notice to Sissle because I had had enough of his band. I would have considered staying longer if he had offered me a raise but he would have preferred cutting off his right hand than to ask me if I would stay for a raise in my salary.

In the meantime, I had been receiving letters and telegrams from Rodger Kay asking me to hurry back to New York because he was going to take a combo into a new club and wanted me to join him. I played my last job with Sissle in Louisville, Ky. and taken an early morning train to Cincinnati, where I stayed a couple of days to visit my parents and the rest of my family. Saw a few old friends and returned to the Apple.

Things had happened quite fast and unforunately for Rodger. He had formed an orchestra with a white drummer, Jim Chapin, a Canadian pianist whose name was Bill something, a well known white bassist named Sid Wales and Jem Davis, an alto man that had a style on the order of Pete Brown. Lem and Pete both lived in Brooklyn.
